extraction.name: SeamlessAlign
extraction.description: An automatically aligned multilingual and multimodal translation corpus covering 37 languages and approximately 470,000 hours: approximately 200,000 hours of English speech paired with non-English text, 240,000 hours of non-English speech paired with English text, and 29,000 hours of non-English speech paired with English speech. Metadata is released to enable reconstruction of the full corpus.
extraction.creator: Seamless Communication
extraction.citeAs: Seamless Communication et al. SeamlessM4T: Massively Multilingual & Multimodal Machine Translation. arXiv:2308.11596v3, 25 October 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: SeamlessAlign was created through parallel data mining. The authors started with 4 million hours of raw audio from a publicly available repository of crawled web data and the sentence-segmented text dataset used by NLLB. Audio was downloaded, cleaned, segmented, and assigned language labels. Speech segments and text sentences were encoded into a shared SONAR embedding space, then compared across languages to identify speech-text and speech-speech translation pairs. Mining focused on 37 target languages.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For SeamlessAlign, some English-speech-to-non-English-text directions were not mined because of the size of the English audio and foreign text collections; these directions are marked with dashes in Table 10 and left for future work. Separately, the paper explicitly reports missing CVSS evaluation samples in Catalan, German, Estonian, French, Italian, Mongolian, Persian, and Portuguese. In Fleurs, quality review means that some sentences lack recordings and some lack all three speaker recordings.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw audio originated from a publicly available repository of crawled web data, totaling 4 million hours, approximately 1 million of which were English. Text came entirely from the same dataset deployed in NLLB, using the same sources, cleaning, and filtering steps.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio was resampled to 16 kHz and over-segmented into overlapping candidate splits, roughly increasing the number of potential segments eightfold. SONAR encoders mapped speech and text into a shared fixed-size embedding space. FAISS indexed these embeddings for bidirectional nearest-neighbor retrieval. Global mining used a margin criterion with 16 nearest neighbors and a score threshold of 1.15 to construct translation pairs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text preprocessing reused NLLB's sources, cleaning, sentence segmentation, and filtering through Stopes. Audio preprocessing deduplicated file URLs, downloaded and resampled files to 16 kHz, and removed non-speech data using a bespoke audio event detection model. Silero Voice Activity Detection produced shorter segments, the authors' speech language-identification model labeled the audio, and overlapping splits were generated for mining. Language-specific LID thresholds were chosen so that the estimated probability of a correct classification exceeded that of an incorrect classification. For downstream X2T training, the authors selected the highest-scoring SeamlessAlign pairs, capped at 400 hours per direction for 33 into-English directions and 200 hours per direction for 29 from-English directions. Additional training-data filters removed toxicity-imbalanced pairs, utterances shorter than 0.1 seconds or longer than 50 seconds, text longer than 250 subwords, and text exceeding specified proportions of emojis, punctuation, or spaces.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: SeamlessAlign translation alignments were produced automatically through SONAR similarity-based mining, with a margin threshold of 1.15 selected after human inspection. Speech language labels were generated by the authors' LID100 model. For downstream S2ST training, an in-house ASR model generated target-speech transcriptions and XLS-R-based unit extraction generated discrete acoustic targets. Separately, human evaluation of model outputs used XSTS semantic-similarity ratings and MOS ratings of speech clarity, sound quality, and naturalness. XSTS annotators completed English practice evaluations with score justifications, ignored non-speech tags, pauses, and noises, and evaluated calibration items intermixed with ordinary items. Human toxicity analysis classified detected items as true or false positives.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For mined alignments, the authors chose a SONAR margin threshold of 1.15 after human inspection; released metadata allows users to tune the threshold to balance corpus size against alignment quality. For the separate XSTS human evaluations, disagreement of at least two score points among three annotators triggered two additional ratings. The median rating was retained per item, and direction-level scores averaged these medians. Moderated cross-lingual calibration was used to reduce language-level annotator biases, and bootstrap resampling estimated uncertainty due to finite annotator samples. MOS evaluations retained item-level medians but did not use disagreement-triggered additional ratings or calibration. Human toxicity analysis checked automatic detections for true and false positives.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Not specified for SeamlessAlign's automatic alignments. For separate human evaluation of translation outputs, XSTS used 3 annotators per item, increasing to 5 when score disagreement was at least 2 points. MOS generally used 3 annotators per item, but Catalan, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Korean, Portuguese, Romanian, Swahili, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Urdu, and Vietnamese used 1 annotator per item.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SONAR speech and text encoders; Stopes mining pipelines; FAISS similarity-search library; the authors' ECAPA-TDNN-based LID100 speech language-identification model. For downstream training labels: NLLB-200-3.3B for translation pseudo-labeling, multilingual text-to-unit models for acoustic-unit pseudo-labeling, XLS-R-1B with k-means for acoustic-unit extraction, and an in-house ASR model for target-speech transcription.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Metadata for the full approximately 470,000-hour SeamlessAlign corpus, using a SONAR threshold of 1.15, and mining code in Stopes are open-sourced. The current corpus covers 37 languages; scaling mining to all 100 SeamlessM4T languages and mining additional directions are left for future iterations. No updating schedule or deprecation policy is stated.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speech language labels are assigned during collection. The model card states that training data were mined from publicly available web sources and that personally identifiable information may not have been entirely eliminated despite extensive cleaning. Separately, Fleurs reader gender was used when pairing human-reference recordings, with same-gender pairings achieved for 53% of items and mixed-gender pairings for the remaining 47%.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The released corpus and tools are intended to support further multilingual speech-translation research. The paper discusses potential improvements in multilingual communication, information access, and accessibility for people with limited literacy or visual impairments, as well as benefits for languages with multiple or nonstandardized writing systems. It also warns that improved access may make communities with lower digital literacy more vulnerable to misinformation or scams if the work is misappropriated, and that toxic, biased, or false translations can adversely affect important decisions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Gender representation analysis included SeamlessAlign mined training data and found an overrepresentation of masculine lexica compared with feminine lexica in the analyzed datasets. This analysis used a limited English lexical vocabulary and linguistic gender markers as proxies for gender representation. The paper also reports that language coverage and available data volumes differ substantially across languages.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: SeamlessAlign mining covers 37 languages rather than all 100 system languages, and some English-speech-to-non-English-text directions remain unmined. Parallel mining can produce noisy alignments and requires filtering. Incorrect speech language identification can prevent useful segments from being aligned or introduce noise, with confusions observed between closely related languages. VAD-based over-segmentation increases the number of segments eightfold, introduces embedding-space noise, and increases computational demand; pause-based segments may not correspond to semantically coherent sentences. The released metadata covers the full corpus, whereas model training used selected higher-scoring subsets. Gender-representation results rely on limited lexical lists and cannot necessarily generalize to other noun sets. Personally identifiable information may remain despite cleaning.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training multilingual speech-to-text and speech-to-speech translation systems. SeamlessAlign subsets were combined with human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data to train SeamlessM4T. Released metadata and Stopes mining code enable researchers to reconstruct the corpus, create similar alignments, and tune alignment-score thresholds for their tasks, balancing dataset size against alignment quality.
